101: Hill notes that in today's Changed World, the order of the day is SPECIALIZATION. He quotes Robert P. Moore, a Columbia University administrator, who states that companies particularly seek candidates who specialized in some field—business school graduates with accounting and statistics training, engineers, journalists, architects, chemists, and outstanding senior class leaders. The graduate active on campus with a personality that gets along with all kinds of people has a decided edge over the strictly academic student. Some receive several job offers, as many as six. Moore notes most companies look not only at academic records but activity records and personalities. One leading industrial company wrote: 'We are interested primarily in finding people who can make exceptional progress in management work. For this reason we emphasize qualities of character, intelligence and personality far more than specific educational background.' Moore proposes 'apprenticing' students in offices, stores, and industrial occupations during summer vacation, urging that after two or three years, every student should choose a definite future course.
102: Moore continues, urging colleges and universities to face the practical consideration that all professions and occupations now demand specialists, and to accept more direct responsibility for vocational guidance. Hill identifies night schools in most large cities as reliable sources of specialized training, and correspondence schools for training anywhere U.S. mails reach. America also has abundant self-study books, courses, and materials. An advantage of self-study is flexibility—studying during spare time, work breaks, or travel. Hill observes that anything acquired without effort and without cost is generally unappreciated and often discredited—perhaps why we get so little from public schools. The SELF-DISCIPLINE from a definite study program compensates for wasted free educational opportunity. He shares a personal story: enrolling in a home study advertising course, he stopped after eight or ten lessons, but the school kept sending bills. Since legally obligated to pay, he decided to complete the lessons for his money's worth. Later he discovered the school's efficient collection system was valuable training—being forced to pay, he completed the course, and the advertising training later earned him significant money.
103: Hill identifies a weakness in the public school system: IT IS FREE. People value only that which has a price—free schools and libraries don't impress because they're free. This is why many need additional training after starting work, and why EMPLOYERS GIVE GREATER CONSIDERATION to employees who participate in self-study and professional development. Employers know that anyone with ambition to sacrifice spare time for self-improvement has leadership qualities. This isn't charity but sound business judgment. Hill identifies the universal weakness with no remedy: LACK OF AMBITION. People who schedule spare time for self-improvement seldom remain at the bottom long—their action opens the upward climb, removes obstacles, and gains the interest of those with power to provide OPPORTUNITY. Home study training especially suits employed people who need additional specialized knowledge but can't return to school. Changed economic conditions have forced thousands to find new income sources, often requiring specialized knowledge and complete occupational changes. Just as merchants replace non-selling merchandise with in-demand items, people marketing personal services must also adapt. Hill introduces Stuart Austin Wier, who prepared as a construction engineer until the Depression limited his market.
104: Stuart Austin Wier took inventory of himself, decided to change professions to law, went back to school, and took special courses to prepare as a corporation lawyer. Despite the ongoing Depression, he completed training, passed the bar, and quickly built a lucrative practice in Dallas, Texas—actually turning away clients. Hill adds that Wier was past 40 and married when he returned to school, anticipating alibis of 'I have a family to support' or 'I'm too old.' By carefully selecting highly specialized courses at well-prepared colleges, Wier completed in two years what most law students require four years for. Hill declares: 'IT PAYS TO KNOW HOW TO PURCHASE KNOWLEDGE!' He states that whoever stops studying after finishing school is doomed to mediocrity. The way of success is continuous pursuit of knowledge. He then tells the story of a grocery store salesman who lost his position during the Depression. Having some bookkeeping experience, he took a special accounting course, familiarized himself with latest bookkeeping and office equipment, and started his own business. Beginning with his former employer, he contracted with 100+ small merchants to keep books at nominal monthly fees. He set up a portable office in a delivery truck equipped with modern bookkeeping equipment, eventually creating a fleet of these 'offices on wheels' with a large staff.
105: Hill explains that specialized knowledge plus imagination were the ingredients of the bookkeeping business. The owner soon paid income tax almost ten times what the former grocer employer paid—the Depression's temporary adversity proved a blessing in disguise. The business began with an IDEA that Hill himself supplied. He then suggests another idea with income potential: the woman (a typist clever at hand lettering) who helped prepare the bookkeeper's attractive portfolio saw in it the making of a new profession—preparing marketing materials for personal services. She prepared a 'Marketing Plan for Personal Services' and, spurred by its success, turned to solving a similar problem for her son who had just finished college but couldn't find a market for his services. The plan she originated was the finest specimen of merchandising personal services Hill had ever seen. The portfolio contained nearly 50 pages of beautifully typed, organized information about her son's native ability, schooling, personal experiences, and other information. It included a complete description of the position desired and a word picture of the exact plan he would use in filling it.
106: The portfolio's preparation required several weeks. The woman sent her son to the public library daily for information to sell his services to best advantage, and to all competitors of his prospective employer to gather vital information about their business methods—which proved valuable in forming his plan. The finished portfolio contained more than half a dozen excellent suggestions for the prospective employer's benefit (which the company later adopted). Hill asks: 'Why go to all this trouble?' and answers dramatically: 'DOING A THING WELL NEVER IS TROUBLE! THE PLAN...HELPED HIM GET THE JOB FOR WHICH HE APPLIED, AT THE FIRST INTERVIEW, AT A SALARY FIXED BY HIMSELF.' Moreover, the position didn't require starting at the bottom—he began as a junior executive at an executive's salary. The planned presentation clipped off no less than ten years he would have needed to reach that position starting from the bottom. Hill critiques the 'start at the bottom' idea: too many who begin at the bottom never lift their heads high enough to be seen by OPPORTUNITY. The outlook from the bottom is not bright—it kills ambition, creates 'getting into a rut' through daily routine habit. This is why it pays to start one or two steps above the bottom, forming the HABIT of looking around, observing how others get ahead, and seeing and embracing OPPORTUNITY.
107: Hill introduces Dan Halpin as an example. During college, Halpin was manager of the famous National Championship Notre Dame football team under Knute Rockne. Perhaps inspired by Rockne to aim high and NOT MISTAKE TEMPORARY DEFEAT FOR FAILURE (as Carnegie inspired his lieutenants), Halpin finished college during the Depression when jobs were scarce. After a fling at investment banking and motion pictures, he took the first opening with potential—selling hearing aids on commission. ANYONE COULD START THERE, AND HALPIN KNEW IT, but it opened the door. After nearly two years in a job he disliked, he aimed at assistant sales manager and got the position. That step placed him high enough to see greater opportunity and for OPPORTUNITY TO SEE HIM. He made such a fine record selling hearing aids that A.M. Andrews, chairman of Dictograph Products Company (a competitor), wanted to know about 'that man, Dan Halpin' taking big sales from Dictograph. Andrews sent for Halpin, and after the interview, Halpin was the new sales manager of Dictograph's Acousticon Division. To test him, Andrews went to Florida for three months, leaving Halpin to sink or swim. He did not sink! Knute Rockne's spirit of 'All the world loves a winner, and has no time for a loser' inspired him.
108: Halpin put so much into his job that he was eventually elected vice president of the company and general manager of the Acousticon and Silent Radio Division—a job most executives would be proud to earn through ten years of loyal effort. Halpin achieved it in little more than six months! Hill credits both Andrews and Halpin with IMAGINATION—Andrews for seeing a go-getter, Halpin for REFUSING TO COMPROMISE WITH LIFE BY ACCEPTING A JOB HE DIDN'T WANT. This is a major point: we rise to high positions or remain at the bottom BECAUSE OF CONDITIONS WE CAN CONTROL IF WE DESIRE TO CONTROL THEM. Both success and failure are largely results of HABIT. Hill believes Halpin's association with Knute Rockne planted the same DESIRE to excel that made Notre Dame football world famous—hero worship is helpful provided one worships a WINNER. Hill's belief in business associations was demonstrated when his son Blair negotiated with Halpin for a position. Halpin offered about half what a rival company would pay. Hill used parental pressure to accept Halpin's offer because he BELIEVES CLOSE ASSOCIATION WITH ONE WHO REFUSES TO COMPROMISE WITH CIRCUMSTANCES HE DOESN'T LIKE IS AN ASSET THAT CAN NEVER BE MEASURED IN TERMS OF MONEY. The bottom is a monotonous, dreary, unprofitable place—that's why proper planning to circumvent lowly beginnings matters.
109: Hill suggests some readers may find in these IDEAS the nucleus of the riches they DESIRE. Simple IDEAS have been seedlings of great fortunes—Woolworth's Five and Ten Cent Store idea was so simple as to be almost unworthy of consideration, yet it piled up a fortune. There is no fixed price for sound IDEAS. Behind all IDEAS is specialized knowledge, which is more abundant and easily acquired than IDEAS. Capability means IMAGINATION—the quality needed to combine specialized knowledge with IDEAS in the form of ORGANIZED PLANS designed to yield riches. If readers have IMAGINATION, these stories may stimulate an idea sufficient to begin the riches they desire. The IDEA is the main thing; specialized knowledge can be found around any corner. But IMAGINATION is the catalyst that unites a good idea with the specialized knowledge required to translate it into SUCCESS. The chapter ends with a quote: 'Anybody can WISH for riches, and most people do, but only a few know that a definite plan, plus a BURNING DESIRE for wealth, are the only dependable means of accumulating wealth.'
110: This page features a single inspirational quote in large text: 'The only limitation is that which one sets up in one's own mind.' This quote, attributed to Napoleon Hill, serves as a thematic divider between Chapter 4 (Specialized Knowledge) and Chapter 5 (Imagination). It encapsulates a core principle recurring throughout the book: that mental limitations are self-imposed and can be overcome through the proper application of desire, faith, and the other principles.
